readerTitle: Demand rose 30%. Why did fish orders rise 120%?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (해산물 식당, 구독 앱) + 실제 연구 (MIT 맥주 게임, Sterman 1989) + 일상 관찰 (샤워 온도)
insight: 결과가 늦게 보이는 시스템에서는 지금 눈에 보이는 상태가 아니라 이미 오고 있는 것까지 세고 나서 움직여야 과잉 반응을 피한다.
misconception: 결과가 아직 안 보이면 조치가 부족하다는 뜻이니 더 세게 밀어붙여야 한다.

sources.text: Sterman, J. D. (1989). Modeling Managerial Behavior: Misperceptions of Feedback in a Dynamic Decision Making Experiment. Management Science, 35(3), 321–339.
MIT Sloan, The Beer Distribution Game (1960년대 MIT 시스템 다이내믹스 그룹에서 개발)
식당·구독 앱 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 맥주 게임: 수요가 한 번 오른 뒤 유지되는데도 주문과 재고가 크게 출렁였다는 점, 참가자들이 '주문했지만 아직 받지 못한 물량'을 충분히 고려하지 않았다는 점은 Sterman(1989)의 핵심 결과입니다. 게시 전 원문으로 표현을 다시 확인하세요. 개발 시기(1960년대)도 확인 필요.
참가자들이 출렁임의 원인을 고객 수요 변동 탓으로 돌리는 경향이 있었다는 내용은 Sterman의 후속 글에서 자주 언급됩니다. 원문 확인 전까지 카드에는 'often'으로 완화해 적었습니다.

cards.title: Demand rose 30%. Why did fish orders rise 120%?
body: On Wednesday, a seafood restaurant nearly ran out of fish. By Sunday, it had two and a half times more fish than it wanted, and fish doesn't keep.
Nobody was careless. Every order made sense on the day it was placed.

image.label: A walk-in fridge overflowing with fish crates next to an empty one
image.brief: 좌우 분할 일러스트. 왼쪽은 '수요일' 라벨, 거의 빈 냉장고 앞에서 걱정하는 매니저. 오른쪽은 '일요일' 라벨, 생선 상자가 넘쳐나는 같은 냉장고. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: How much fish do you order tonight?
body: A good review lifts daily fish sales from 100 to 130 portions. Orders take 3 days to arrive. You like 100 portions left at closing.
It's Wednesday night. Only 10 are left. You ordered 160 on Monday and 190 on Tuesday. Neither has arrived yet.

options.text: 220: tonight's 130 plus 90 to refill the shelf
options.feedback: It matches what the shelf says, and it's what you did Monday and Tuesday. But the 350 portions already coming refill the shelf by Friday, so this order lands Saturday in a full fridge.
Thursday's and Friday's deliveries bring you back to 100 by Friday night. Saturday's delivery only needs to cover Saturday.
You're right that plenty is on the way. But with no Saturday delivery, you'd run 30 portions short on a busy day.

cards.title: What happens if you order by the shelf
body: Say the manager ordered 220 on Wednesday, the same way as the days before. Here's the fish left at closing each day. The target was 100.
cards.callout: A small, steady change in demand became a big swing in stock.

cards.title: Delays in systems
body: A **delay** is the gap between an action and its visible effect.
When you steer by what you see right now, you keep pushing after enough is already on its way. Then it all arrives at once, and you overshoot.
You know this from a hotel shower. You turn it hotter, nothing happens, you turn it more, and then it scalds you.

image.label: A shower dial turned too far, with a timeline showing water warming late
image.brief: 샤워 다이얼을 여러 번 돌리는 손과 그 아래 시간축 그래프. '돌린 시점'과 '물이 뜨거워진 시점' 사이에 간격 표시, 온도 선이 목표를 넘어 출렁임.

cards.title: The Beer Game
body: MIT has used a simple classroom game since the 1960s. Players each run one stage of a beer supply chain: retailer, wholesaler, distributor, brewery. Orders and shipments take a few weeks to arrive.
Customer demand rises once and then stays put. Yet orders and stock swing wildly up the chain.
In a 1989 study, John Sterman found players **largely ignored orders they had placed but not yet received**. Players often blamed the swings on customers, though demand barely moved.

image.label: Four players in a chain passing orders, with stock levels swinging
image.brief: 테이블에 앉은 네 사람이 일렬로 주문서를 전달하는 장면. 각자 머리 위에 재고 그래프가 있고, 뒤로 갈수록 출렁임이 커짐. 실제 맥주 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Delays hide in most decisions.
body: Look for the gap between doing something and seeing it work:
list: **Hiring:** weeks to recruit, months before a new person is fully up to speed
**Marketing:** a campaign may bring customers long after it ends
**Prices:** many customers react only when they next renew or reorder
**Training:** skills show up in results long after the course
cards.callout: The longer the delay, the easier it is to act twice for one problem.

cards.title: Waiting isn't always the answer.
body: Delays punish impatience, but they also punish slowness. If you wait out every signal, you react late and the problem grows.
The fix is to know roughly how long each delay is, keep track of what's already in the pipeline, and make smaller moves.
Better still, shorten the delay. Smaller, more frequent deliveries would have kept the restaurant's swings much smaller.

cards.title: Now it's a subscription app.
body: Your app offers a 30-day free trial. You redesigned the first-day setup screens. Two weeks later, new paid subscriptions are flat.
Your team wants to roll back. What do you do?

options.text: Roll back now, since the numbers haven't moved
options.feedback: No trial that started under the new design has reached its payment date yet. Flat paid numbers can't tell you anything about the redesign.

options.text: Keep it, watch how many new trial users finish setup, and judge paid conversions once the first trials end
options.feedback: You get an early signal now and the real answer in a few weeks, without undoing work that hasn't had time to show.

options.text: Keep it, and add a launch discount to lift paid signups
options.feedback: The test stays alive, but now two changes overlap. When results arrive, you won't know which one worked.

cards.title: Before acting again, count what's already on its way.
body: When results lag, what you see today reflects old decisions. Steer by the shelf alone and you'll overshoot.
**Try it today:** pick one change you made recently. Write down how long it should take to show results, and what's already in the pipeline.
